turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of Inside Engineering. I'm Sarah, the chief information security officer here, and I'm joined by David, who runs our engineering organization. Today we're going to talk honestly about our security roadmap for the next year. David, welcome.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Thanks, Sarah. I should say up front that we don't agree on everything, which is probably what makes this worth recording.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Exactly. Let's start with what happened last quarter, because it shaped a lot of my thinking. For listeners who missed the internal report, a contractor on our billing team received a phishing email that looked like a password reset from our payroll provider. They entered their credentials, and within an hour someone logged into our VPN from an IP address in another country.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: And to be clear, the attacker didn't get far. Our monitoring flagged the login because it came from an unusual location, and the account was disabled within about forty minutes. But it was a wake-up call.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: It was. The part that worried me most was not the phishing email. People will always click on something eventually. What worried me was that once someone was on the VPN, the network basically trusted them. That contractor account could reach dozens of internal systems it had no business touching, including an old reporting server with customer data.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: That old reporting server has been on my list to decommission for two years, so I'll take some of the blame there.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: That's why my main proposal for this year is that we replace the VPN with a zero trust architecture. The idea is simple. No device and no user gets trusted just because it's inside the network. Every request to every internal application is authenticated, checked against the health of the device, and limited to the minimum access the person actually needs.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: I understand the goal, and I agree with the principle. Where I disagree is the timeline. You want to remove the VPN completely by the end of this year. My team is also committed to shipping the new patient scheduling product in the same period. If every engineer has to change how they reach staging environments, databases, and internal dashboards at the same time, we will lose weeks of productivity.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I hear that. But the risk doesn't wait for our product calendar.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Sure, but a failed rollout is also a risk. My counterproposal is a phased approach. Start with the applications that hold customer data, like the billing system and the reporting tools, and put those behind the zero trust access proxy first. Leave the engineering tools on the VPN until after the scheduling launch, and then migrate them.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I can live with phases, as long as the first phase covers everything with patient or payment data, and as long as we put a date on the final phase. Otherwise the VPN will still be here in five years.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: That's fair. Let's put a date on it.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Good. The second topic is multi-factor authentication. Today we require it for email and the VPN, but not for a lot of internal tools. I want hardware security keys for everyone with administrator access, and app-based multi-factor authentication for everyone else, with no exceptions for contractors.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: No objection from me there. Honestly, the security keys are easier for engineers than typing codes from a phone. The only question is budget. How much are we talking about?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Around two hundred people need keys, and we want two per person in case one is lost. So roughly four hundred keys at about fifty dollars each, which is twenty thousand dollars. Compared to the cost of one serious incident, that's nothing.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Agreed. Consider it approved.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Should we also do more phishing training? The contractor incident started with an email, after all.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Some, but I don't want to rely on training alone. We'll run a phishing simulation every quarter, and instead of shaming people who click, we'll make it very easy to report suspicious emails with a single button. The goal is fast reporting. If one person reports a phishing email within five minutes, we can pull it out of every other inbox before most people even open it.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: I like that framing. Rewarding reporting instead of punishing clicks.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Third topic, and this is the one with a hard deadline. Our SOC 2 Type Two audit window begins on September first. The auditors will look at access reviews, change management, and how we handle incidents over the entire observation period. Anything we fix after September first won't count for this year's report.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: That's the date that actually scares me. Several of our biggest hospital customers told us they won't renew without a clean SOC 2 report.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Which is why I want the access reviews automated before then. Right now, a manager gets a spreadsheet every quarter and clicks approve on everything. That isn't a real review. I'd like a tool that pulls the actual permissions from our identity provider and from each application, and highlights anything unusual, like a contractor with administrator rights.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: I'd add one more item to that list. Our Kubernetes clusters. Right now too many engineers have cluster administrator permissions, mostly for convenience. Before the audit, I want to move everyone to namespace level roles and keep cluster administrator access for a small on-call group.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: I'm glad you raised that, because it's the principle of least privilege applied to infrastructure. And the secrets stored in those clusters are exactly what an attacker would look for.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: We should also run a penetration test before the audit rather than after. If an outside firm finds something, I'd rather fix it while there's still time.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Agreed. Let's schedule the penetration test for June, which gives us July and August to fix the findings before the September date.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: What about ransomware? Our customers ask about it more than anything else in their security questionnaires.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Our backups are the most important defense. We have daily backups, but until recently they were stored in the same cloud account as production. If an attacker got administrator access to that account, they could delete the backups along with everything else. We have now moved copies to a separate account with immutable storage, so nobody can delete them for thirty days, not even us.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: And we tested a restore, which is the part people usually skip. It took about six hours to restore the main database, which is longer than I'd like.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: That's our next improvement. Our target is to restore critical systems in under two hours. We'll practice it as part of an incident response exercise in the fall.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: And logging? If something does happen, will we even know what the attacker touched?

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Today, only partly. Logs from our cloud accounts and the identity provider go to a central system, but the Kubernetes audit logs are kept for only seven days. I want every log kept for at least one year, which is also something the auditors will ask about.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: So let me summarize where we landed, because we started out disagreeing. Sarah proposed replacing the VPN with zero trust access. I disagreed with doing it all at once, and we agreed on phases, starting with the systems that hold patient and payment data.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: And we're putting a date on the final phase. The engineering tools move off the VPN by the end of March next year, after the scheduling launch.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Plus hardware security keys for administrators, least privilege roles in Kubernetes, a penetration test in June, and faster backup restores.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: And all of it is tied to the audit deadline we discussed earlier, September first. If there is one message for everyone listening, it's this. Assume someone will get in eventually, and design your systems so that when they do, they can't reach much.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Thanks, Sarah. This was a good conversation, even the parts where we argued.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: Especially those parts. Thanks, everyone, for listening.
